events.c: The aircraft arrived at JFK from Athens. Its incoming crew reported no operating problems.
Staff resolved a baggage concern that had delayed departure, confirming the passenger linked to the bag was aboard.
The crew requested pushback from the gate. The air conditioning had been running on the ground.
With three engines started, the crew requested clearance to taxi.
The crew started the remaining engine while taxiing and completed the checks.
Controllers cleared the aircraft onto the runway to wait, warning of disturbed air behind a Boeing 757.
Controllers cleared the aircraft for takeoff from runway 22R.
The aircraft lifted off at about 8:19 p.m. local time.
The crew contacted departure control as the aircraft began climbing.
Boston Center took over air traffic control as the aircraft continued climbing.
Controllers cleared a climb to 19,000 feet, asking the crew to pass through 15,000 feet quickly.
Controllers changed the clearance, instructing the crew to maintain 13,000 feet.
An altitude alert sounded as the aircraft reached its assigned height.
The captain noticed an unusual fuel flow reading. Its connection to the later ignition was not established.
Controllers cleared a climb to 15,000 feet. The crew called for more engine power.
The captain in the right seat acknowledged the climb clearance. This was the last radio acknowledgment.
The flight engineer confirmed the power setting. Engine power then rose as the aircraft climbed.
Islip radar received its last aircraft reply. Other radar sites continued tracking it briefly.
The flight recorder stopped recording data. The exact moment it lost power is uncertain.
Radar received the aircraft's last identifying reply. Later echoes carried no aircraft identity or altitude.
An explosion in the fuel tank between the wings began the breakup. The exact ignition time is unknown.
A brief, loud sound preceded the end of the cockpit recording.
The nose is estimated to have separated about three to five seconds after the initial explosion.
The remaining aircraft is estimated to have briefly climbed and changed direction after losing its nose.
The outer wings are estimated to have failed about 34 seconds after the initial explosion.
A nearby airline captain reported seeing an explosion. The report does not establish when the initial explosion happened.
The center section is estimated to have failed near the left wing, leaving pieces falling without control.
The main wreckage hit the ocean an estimated 47–54 seconds after the explosion. The nose fell separately.
Aircraft and boats responded to the burning wreckage that evening. No survivors were found.
Both recorders were recovered on July 24. The flight recorder's tape was readable.
The FBI ended its active criminal investigation, announcing it had found no evidence of a criminal cause.
Investigators found a tank explosion, probably ignited by excessive voltage through fuel gauge wiring. The source remains uncertain.
Petitioners challenged the findings using radar, witness accounts, and physical evidence. Some had participated in the original investigation.
Investigators heard the petitioners' case, including an eyewitness account. The meeting did not establish a new cause.
Investigators rejected the request to reconsider after reviewing radar arguments and additional witness accounts.
Investigators announced plans to retire the reconstructed wreckage and document it digitally before destruction, as agreed with families.
Judicial Watch announced FBI records describing early leads and claims of responsibility. These did not verify an attack.
The Clinton Library announced newly processed records. No new official cause determination was identified.

one_line: A fuel tank explosion broke apart a Boeing 747 shortly after takeoff from New York.
status_why: Investigators established a fuel tank explosion and ruled out a missile or bomb. The exact ignition source remains unknown.
